transcript.text: There's water all over the kitchen floor coming from under my Beko washing machine and its gone under the units to where the plug is, the machine is still going. What do I do?

Water near the plug or socket is dangerous. Please don't touch the plug, socket or machine if they or your hands are wet. If you can do it safely, switch off the circuit at the consumer unit (fuse box), keep away from the water, and don't use the machine again until a qualified electrician or appliance engineer has checked it. Stop the machine now. Because water has reached the plug area, do not touch the plug, socket, machine controls or any water around them. 1. Isolate the washing-machine circuit at the consumer unit/fuse box if you can do so without standing in water. Do not pull the plug out.
2. Turn off the washing-machine water supply tap only if you can reach it without going near wet electrics.
3. Keep people and pets away from the wet area. Once the supply is isolated, use towels to contain water away from the socket area; do not move the machine.
4. Do not use the machine again, even if the leak stops. It needs a qualified appliance engineer to check it before it is powered up again, as water has reached an electrical area. The common causes are a pump/filter or internal hose leak underneath, a drain-hose connection, or a leak from the dispenser, door seal or filling system. The water’s appearance and the point in the cycle when it started will help identify which one, but do not run another programme to test it.
ok I can reach the fuse box in the hall, the floor there is dry. I'm standing in socks on the wet kitchen floor right now though, should I get off it first? the machine is still running

Yes — get off the wet floor first. Do not walk through it in socks. Step onto a dry area without touching the machine, plug, socket or water, then go to the dry hall and switch off the washing-machine circuit at the consumer unit. Do not touch or unplug the machine afterwards, and do not use it again. Because water has reached the plug area, it needs a qualified appliance engineer to inspect it before it is powered up. Once the circuit is off, the more likely leak sources are the pump/filter or drain-hose area underneath, with the dispenser, door seal or an internal hose also possible. The engineer can trace the source safely; it is not safe to run a test cycle or open the filter while there is water near the electrics.
ok I'm getting off the wet floor now and heading to the hall. will switch off at the fuse box. then what? the water's still coming out I think

If water is still coming out after the power is isolated, it may be incoming water from the supply side, or water draining from the machine. 1. From a dry area, turn off the washing-machine water tap if it is safely reachable without approaching the wet socket/plug area. If it is not, use the home’s main stopcock instead, if you know where it is and can reach it safely.
2. 3. Keep the circuit switched off. Once the water flow has stopped and the area is electrically isolated, contain water from the dry edge with towels only where you can do so without getting near the socket area.
4. Do not restart or plug in the machine. Water has reached the electrical area, so it needs a qualified appliance engineer to inspect the machine before any power is restored to it. If the socket, wiring or units remain wet, an electrician may also be needed. The likely sources are an inlet/fill connection if it keeps feeding water with power off, or an internal hose, pump/filter housing, or drain-hose connection if it is only emptying what was already in the machine.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.

ok I'm in the hall and the fuse box is here. which switch do I turn off? I don't know which one is the washing machine, can I just switch them all off? the tap is behind the machine near the wet plug so I don't want to go near it

Yes. From the dry hall, switch off the consumer unit’s clearly marked main switch if there is one; that will isolate the whole home. If there is no obvious main switch, it is reasonable to switch off all the individual breakers/RCD switches. Do not go back to the tap behind the machine: it is too close to the wet plug area. If water continues to flow after the electricity is isolated, the priority is stopping the water at the home’s main stopcock, but only if you know it is somewhere dry and can reach it without entering the wet kitchen. If you cannot safely do that, call an emergency plumber/water service. The continuing water could be an inlet/fill connection still feeding water, or water escaping from the pump, filter, drain hose or an internal hose. Because water has reached the electrical area, the washing machine must not be used again until a qualified appliance engineer has checked it; if the socket or wiring got wet, arrange an electrician as well.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
there's no main switch I can see that's labelled, just a row of little switches. ok so I switch them all off? and then do I just leave the machine and wait for my partner, he's home in 2 hours?

Yes. From where you are standing in the dry hall, switch all the little breaker switches to OFF if there is no clearly identified washing-machine circuit. That may turn off the whole home, but it is the sensible option here. Do not go back to the machine, plug, socket or tap behind it. If the water is still flowing after the electricity is off, do not simply wait two hours: close the home’s main stopcock only if it is in a dry, safely reachable place. If you cannot safely stop the water, call an emergency plumber or your water supplier’s emergency line now. If the flow stops, you can leave the machine where it is and wait for your partner, keeping everyone out of the kitchen wet area. Do not restore power or use the washer again. It will need a qualified appliance engineer, and the socket/wiring may need an electrician if they have got wet. The continuing leak could be from the incoming water supply, or from a pump/filter, drain hose or internal hose underneath; it cannot be safely traced while the area is wet.
[Safety panel] An appliance that keeps tripping your electrics — or that smells of burning or has scorch marks — may have an electrical fault. Stop using it, switch it off and unplug it, don't keep resetting it, and have it checked by a qualified electrician or appliance engineer.
